the volume shows a young and attractive Mrs Mason at what appears to be the entrance
to a walled garden, her arms outspread over her two young charges, the group framed
by Blakean climbing plants to right and left. The caption is borrowed from the govern-
ess’s exhortation to the girls in chapter 1, ‘Look what a fine morning it is — Insects, Birds,
Animals, are all enjoying existence’, an affirmation of natural harmony based in mutual
pleasure which might stand as epigraph to the first two parts of SP. In the Stories, the gar-
den and surrounding countryside serve as an important scene of Mrs Mason’s instruction,
which includes a didactic comparison between the tulip and the rose (ch. vii) as well as
advice on the humane disposal of harmful insects (ch. i), which the Lady of SP seems to
have made her own (ii 41–8).
